title: Chapter 3. When a person has enough VAT coupons to buy what they need

blocks.text: If humanoids work for humans, an immediate question remains, the kind asked in the bread queue and not at a conference: what, then, is used to buy what is necessary? Pedro answers with an image of his own, which is not a law in force or an approved programme, and which this book presents as what it is — a proposal: that a person should have enough VAT coupons to buy what they need.

blocks.text: VAT exists. In Spain, the value-added tax is a tax on consumption. The tax agency applies, as a rule, a standard rate of 21 per cent, a reduced rate of 10 and a super-reduced rate of 4, according to what is bought, in line with Law 37/1992 and the rules that develop it. In practice it is paid by the person who buys: bread, oil, transport, so many everyday goods and services carry that charge, visible or built into the price. Those who have little pay it too. At the till, the tax does not ask whether the four coins of chapter 1 will stretch. It asks what is being taken away.

blocks.text: That is the paradox Pedro wants to turn around. A levy that today is loaded onto the act of buying could become, in his idea, the right to obtain what is necessary. Not a luxury. Not a prize. What a person needs in order to live: to eat, to keep warm, to be cared for, to have a home, to move, to look after others. Enough coupons. The word “enough” is the centre. This is not about filling the midnight trolley of which this book will speak later. It is about no one having to rent out the day in order to deserve a kilo of tomatoes.

blocks.text: The coupons are not, today, in anyone's purse under that name and with that function. In real life there are bonuses, allowances, cheques, benefits, each with its rules and its limits. This chapter does not deny them or confuse them with the proposal. The proposal is something else: a universal right to what is necessary, expressed in coupons tied to the VAT system, so that basic consumption ceases to be a privilege of whoever has a wage and ceases to be a charity. The tax that falls on things would return, in the form of a coupon, to whoever needs them. The circle closes in a way other than that of the four coins: a life is not sold in order to buy bread; bread is recognised as what it is, a right, and is made effective.

blocks.text: Who decides what is “necessary”? The question is a serious one, and should not be brushed aside with an adjective. The necessary is not the same in every house, or at every age, or in every body. Chapter 8 will dream of a food according to each person's biological needs. Here, lower down, a humble rule is enough: the necessary is that without which a person cannot live in dignity — food, a roof, care, the essentials of daily life. What goes beyond that, if it does, is no longer the business of this coupon. The coupon is not there to manufacture millionaires. It is there so that no one is left off the table. The next chapter will say what then happens to fortune and to power.

blocks.text: In a district such as this, the image can be brought down to earth without effort. A market, boxes of tomatoes, the oil, the fish, the bread. Today one pays, and in the price goes the VAT. Tomorrow, in the dream of these pages, one would have coupons enough to take home what the household needs, without having had to prove, that morning, that the hours had been sold. The seller would not lose the trade: the coupon would be as valid as the coin, or more so, because it would represent a right and not a luxury. The garden and the market would still be a market, in the good sense of the word: a place where things circulate. What would change is the blackmail.

blocks.text: Some will fear abuse, or disorder, or that “if the necessary is given, no one will do anything.” It is an old fear, and sometimes it serves those who prefer bread to depend on the wage. This book has already said, in chapter 2, that making does not disappear when the obligation to hire oneself out disappears. Craft, care, contribution, the pleasure of doing something well, remain. What is withdrawn is hunger as a whip. A sufficient coupon does not make a society idle: it takes away fear. And fear, when it organises work, organises injustice as well.

blocks.text: Some will ask about the accounts: where the coupon comes from, how tricks are avoided, how the necessary is kept up to date. Those are questions of design, not of principle. The principle is clear and it is Pedro's: each person has enough VAT coupons to buy what they need. The design will come, if one day it is truly wanted, with figures, with checks, with an intelligence that helps people decide — as will be seen later — and with people who vote, not with an office that hands out favours. This essay does not pretend already to have the regulations. Still less does it pretend that the regulations exist. It leaves the principle on the table, beside the four coins, so that the difference can be seen.

blocks.text: Money, if it remains, could go on serving for what is not strictly necessary, or it could fade as the abundance of the machines and, later, of the Moon, makes it less necessary to price everything. The coupon, by contrast, would not price the person. It would price, if anything, the right: this is yours because you live, not because you have earned a wage. It is a change of language. VAT, which today is a percentage on a receipt, would become a passport to the elementary.

blocks.text: From the Mar Menor, coming back from the market, this is understood better than in any treatise. There are people who count the coins in their palm before asking for the fish. There are people who put an item back because the price, with its tax, has got away from them. The sufficient coupon would be, for that scene, a form of everyday peace: taking what is needed without having had to sell oneself. It is not eternal life. It is, barely, not going hungry or without a secure roof for lack of a wage. In the title of this book, the devil's invention was measuring work — and the person — with coins. Pedro's coupon measures no one. It guarantees what should never have been measured: the right to what is needed in order to live.

blocks.text: A last clarification, so as not to mix the coupon with the fever of buying. Chapter 5 will speak of the purchases that plug a hole. Pedro's coupon is not meant for that fever. It is meant for the opposite: so that the necessary does not depend on a craving or a wage, and so that what is surplus stops disguising itself as need. Whoever has a covered plate and a roof will at last be able to tell what is required from what only comforts for a while. VAT, which today is added to almost everything, would then serve the former, not the latter. And the person, with enough coupons, would cease to be a priced customer and become, simply, someone who lives and eats.

blocks.text: On today's receipt, VAT is a percentage. In the proposal, the coupon is a quantity of right. The change looks technical and is political, in the good sense: it affects how what is held in common is shared. One need not be an economist to understand it. It is enough to have left something on the shelf because the wage would not stretch. It is to that person, and not to an abstract scheme, that this chapter is addressed.

blocks.text: The rates of VAT can be argued over, and they are argued over, in every budget. Pedro's principle does not depend on the standard rate being 21 or on bread standing at 4. It depends on the necessary not being left at the mercy of a till receipt. If one day the rates change, the coupon should change with them, so as to remain sufficient. The tool is updated. The right is not.
